title: Selling Property in India as an NRI? The TDS Rules Are Very Different
excerpt: NRI sellers face TDS under Section 195 on the full sale price from the first rupee — not the 1% rule residents get. A Section 197 certificate can bring the deduction down to the actual gain.
body:
• When an NRI sells property in India, the buyer must deduct TDS under Section 195 on the FULL sale price — with no ₹50 lakh threshold and deductions starting from the first rupee, unlike the 1% TDS residents face.
  • Effective rates (base plus surcharge and 4% cess): 12.5% long-term, or 13.00%–14.95% by sale value; 30% short-term, or about 31.2%–35.88%.
  • A lower or nil TDS certificate under Section 197 (Form 13) lets the seller pay tax on the actual gain — but it must be applied for 30–60 days before closing; it cannot reverse tax already deducted.
  • The buyer needs a TAN, must deposit the tax by the 7th of the following month, file Form 27Q quarterly and issue Form 16A to the seller.

Selling a flat in Mumbai or a plot in Bengaluru is complicated enough from 8,000 miles away. For NRIs, there is an extra trap: tax deducted at source works completely differently than for residents — and can lock up far more cash than the seller owes.

The core difference: Section 195 vs Section 194-IA

When a resident sells property above ₹50 lakh, the buyer deducts 1% TDS under Section 194-IA. For an NRI seller, that rule never applies. The transaction moves to Section 195, and three things change at once: the ₹50 lakh threshold disappears, the deduction is calculated on the entire sale consideration rather than the profit, and the buyer needs a Tax Deduction Account Number (TAN) instead of just a PAN.

On a ₹2 crore NRI sale, the buyer deducts on the full ₹2 crore — not on a ₹40 lakh gain. The TDS almost always exceeds the final tax bill, recoverable only as a refund on filing an Indian return.

The rates, checked

For property held over 24 months — long-term — the base TDS rate is 12.5%. With surcharge and the 4% cess, that works out to 13.00% below ₹50 lakh, 14.30% between ₹50 lakh and ₹1 crore, and 14.95% at ₹1 crore and above. For property held 24 months or less — short-term — the base is 30%, or roughly 31.2%, 34.32% and 35.88% across the same slabs.

Caution: older guides quote 20% for long-term TDS — that was pre-July-2024; the current base is 12.5%. (Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, Section 195 becomes Section 393(2).)

What the buyer must do

The buyer carries the compliance burden: obtain a TAN, deduct at the earlier of payment or credit, deposit by the 7th of the following month, file Form 27Q quarterly and issue Form 16A so credit lands against the seller's PAN. From October 1, 2026, a resident individual or HUF buying from a non-resident can use a PAN-based challan without a TAN; companies and other buyers still need one.

Using Form 26QB — the form for resident-seller transactions — for an NRI seller is a common and costly mistake. So is assuming no TDS applies because the sale is below ₹50 lakh.

The certificate that changes the arithmetic

Sellers whose gain is far below the sale price can seek a lower or nil deduction certificate under Section 197 (Form 13), filed before the sale deed is executed. The assessing officer computes the likely gain — after cost, improvements and reinvestment exemptions — and the buyer deducts at the certified rate, often roughly 3–5% or nil.

Timing is everything: turnaround typically runs two to eight weeks, so the application should go in 30 to 60 days before completion, and the certificate must reach the buyer before payment. Once the tax has been deducted, the only way back is a refund on filing.

DTAA relief and getting the money out

Most treaties, including with the U.S. and UK, give India — where the property sits — the primary taxing right, while the seller's home country generally grants a foreign tax credit, limiting double taxation.

Repatriation needs Form 15CA (a self-declaration) and Form 15CB from a chartered accountant, up to $1 million per financial year. Sections 54, 54EC and 54F reinvestment exemptions remain available to NRIs if the reinvestment property is in India.

What to do before you list

Confirm residency status in writing before assuming the 1% rule. Start the Section 197 application early if the gain is well below the price. Write the certificate, TAN and Form 27Q mechanics into the sale agreement so paperwork delays don't stall registration. And confirm specifics with a chartered accountant before closing.
